components.problem: Recursive weight-tied architectures such as Tiny Recursive Models (TRM) have been shown, in prior work, to substitute iterative computation for parameter count when the target problem is a fully-specified refinement task against known dynamics: Jain & Linares (2025, arXiv:2512.16824) recurse over a candidate control sequence and Wijayatunga & Armellin (2026, arXiv:2606.00895) recurse over a departure velocity, both functioning as learned MPC-style correctors that iteratively denoise a numerical answer given an explicit model of the plant. This project asks a mechanistically different question: in model-free continuous-control RL (DDPG/TD3/SAC, no dynamics model) under fixed action delay, can the same weight-tied recursion, applied instead over an observation-augmented history, serve as an implicit memory or state-estimation mechanism that recovers Markov structure lost to delay-induced partial observability? A pilot on Pendulum-v1 with 1-step delay found TRM, a transformer trunk, and a memoryless [256,256] MLP converge to statistically indistinguishable reward, with TRM costing ~18x the wall-clock time of the MLP for no measured benefit -- but this null result was obtained on an arguably trivial POMDP (short horizon, 3-dimensional state, single scalar delay-induced ambiguity) that may not stress any architecture's memory capacity. We state the falsifiable hypothesis under test: TRM's relative advantage in reward-per-fixed-training-budget over a memoryless DNN trunk and over a transformer trunk, all under identical observation-augmentation delay conditioning, is a monotonically non-decreasing function of task complexity (state/action dimensionality, horizon, dynamics coupling). The competing, equally admissible hypothesis is that the advantage remains flat or negative across the complexity range tested, in which case TRM's iterative-recursion inductive bias does not transfer from model-based trajectory refinement to model-free implicit state estimation, and the ~18x overhead is never recovered -- a negative result this proposal treats as a first-class, reportable outcome rather than something to be designed around.
components.method: We test the hypothesis by holding the RL algorithm, the observation-augmentation delay fix, and the training protocol fixed while varying only two things: (1) the actor/critic trunk architecture -- memoryless [256,256] MLP, transformer trunk, and TRM trunk (plus the two available TRM variants, hier6 and singlez, to check whether the recursion-depth/latent-structure choice matters independently of the base TRM-vs-baseline comparison) -- and (2) task complexity, treated as the independent variable and operationalized along three orthogonal axes: state/action dimensionality, effective decision horizon, and dynamics coupling/nonlinearity. All architectures receive the same delay-augmented observation (pending-action queue appended to state) under the same fixed action-delay schedule, isolating the recursion mechanism itself as the only source of architectural difference in how delay-induced partial observability is resolved. The dependent variables are: task reward (mean and variance across seeds at matched training-step budgets, not matched wall-clock, so that architectures are compared on sample efficiency first), wall-clock training time to reach that budget, and parameter count -- the latter two reported as first-class costs rather than footnotes, since the central question is a cost-benefit one. "Does the advantage grow with complexity" is operationalized as a relative-improvement curve: for each environment rung on the complexity ladder, compute (reward_TRM - reward_DNN) and (reward_TRM - reward_transformer) as fractions of the DNN/transformer's own reward range on that task, then plot these deltas against an ordinal complexity index spanning the environment set. A positive, increasing slope across at least two complexity increments, replicated across seeds, is evidence for the growing-advantage hypothesis; a flat or non-monotonic trend is evidence against it. This is a trend-fitting exercise across a small environment ladder, not a single-environment significance test, since the claim under test is inherently about scaling behavior.
components.experiment_design: The complexity ladder extends Pendulum-v1 (rung 0: 3-dim state, 1-dim action, short horizon, moderate nonlinearity -- already implemented) with three further Gymnasium-compatible continuous-control environments, each justified on a distinct, explicitly stated axis: (1) MountainCarContinuous-v0 as a horizon-axis increase -- sparse reward and a much longer effective decision horizon than Pendulum under the same 1-dim action space, stressing the ability to carry delay-relevant information further into the future; this is a classic-control env already Gymnasium-native and should need only a new Hydra env config, not new environment code. (2) BipedalWalker-v3 (Box2D) as a state/action-dimensionality increase -- 24-dim observation, 4-dim continuous action, and stronger dynamics coupling (multi-joint contact dynamics) than Pendulum, requiring a new Hydra env config and verification that the observation-augmentation wrapper generalizes to a 4-dim pending-action queue. (3) A MuJoCo-style env, HalfCheetah-v4 or Hopper-v4, as the top rung on both dimensionality and dynamics-coupling axes (6-17 dim actions, high-dimensional coupled multi-body dynamics), requiring a new Hydra env config plus a MuJoCo dependency/licensing check -- flagged as the rung most likely to need scoping as its own preparatory task before inclusion. The comparison protocol is a full factorial: {DNN, transformer, TRM-base, TRM-hier6, TRM-singlez} architectures x {Pendulum, MountainCarContinuous, BipedalWalker, [HalfCheetah/Hopper if in scope]} environments x {no-delay baseline, 1-step delay, a longer delay e.g. 3-5 steps} delay conditions x >=3 seeds per condition, run as independent PBS jobs on Katana with walltime budgeted <=12h each (higher-complexity envs may need step-budget tuning to fit this ceiling, reported as a constraint, not silently relaxed). Every run logs reward curves, wall-clock time to convergence and to fixed step-budgets, and parameter count, aggregated into the relative-improvement-vs-complexity curve described in Method. If the curve is flat, negative, or non-monotonic -- i.e., TRM's overhead never pays off, or pays off only on the single hardest rung without a clear trend -- this will be reported explicitly as a negative/null scaling result with the same statistical rigor (seed variance, effect sizes) as a positive one, framed as evidence that this architecture's recursive inductive bias, while effective for known-dynamics trajectory refinement in the mandatory prior-art papers, does not transfer to model-free implicit state estimation under delay within the complexity range tested, rather than being attributed to insufficient tuning or reframed post hoc as a partial success.
